order.why_here: The first trust-the-child recursion: each node returns one number, 1 + max of its children.
Same one-visit-per-node walk, but the work is rewiring pointers instead of computing a value.
Recursion over two trees in lockstep, with the None/None and None/node base cases.
Lockstep again, but the two fingers move in mirror image: outer with outer, inner with inner.
Same-tree from every node, then a pre-order string with null markers turns it into substring search.
Return a height up and fold a check into it, with a -1 sentinel that short-circuits.
The full post-order template: return the height up, record left + right on the side.
First problem where the parent passes a fact down: whether the child is a left child.
Carry a running total down the path and test it at the leaves.
Carry the whole path down in one shared list and backtrack it on the way up.
Carry the running maximum of the path down instead of a sum.
Diameter's template with negative values: arms below zero are dropped.
Switch from depth to breadth: a queue with a per-level snapshot.
Uses the level loop to pick one node per row, or DFS with first-visit per depth.
Carry depth and parent down together and compare two nodes' pairs.
Give every node (column, row) coordinates during the walk, then group and sort.
The in-order walk made explicit with a stack, the tool every BST problem needs.
The BST rule is global, so carry (low, high) bounds down.
In-order of a BST is sorted; stop the iterative walk after k pops.
One ordered descent: the first node that splits p and q is the answer.
Without the order, use a post-order found-below-me signal.
Two lazy in-order iterators (predecessor and successor stacks) merged outward from the target.
In-order with a previous pointer finds the two swapped values from the sorted-order breaks.
Reverse a traversal: pre-order picks the root, in-order index splits the ranges.
Rebuild from a depth-annotated pre-order string with a stack of ancestors.
Design both directions: pre-order with null sentinels and a single read cursor.
Same cursor idea when nodes have any number of children: write child counts.
Post-order returns one of three states and a greedy choice is made from the leaves up.
